# Priority queues as frontier managers

A heap maintains the smallest or largest currently available item.
It is the right tool when the next action is determined by one key,
but future insertions can change the frontier.

You should be able to say what one heap entry means. Examples:

```text
(value)                 current candidate number
(end_time)              room that becomes free at this time
(sum, i, j)             pair A[i]+B[j] from stream i at position j
(distance, vertex)      frontier state in Dijkstra
```

The heap does not prove the algorithm by itself. The proof comes from showing
that the smallest or largest key is safe to process next.

# What a binary heap actually stores

A priority queue is an interface: insert an item and extract the smallest or
largest item. A **binary heap** is the usual implementation of that interface.
It is a nearly complete binary tree with an ordering rule.

For a min-heap, every parent is at most its children:

```text
                 2
              /     \
             5       4
           /  \     / \
          9    7   8   6
```

This does **not** mean that every level or the underlying array is sorted.
It guarantees only that the root is globally smallest. After removing it,
the heap repairs the rule and exposes the next smallest item.

## Why heaps are stored in arrays

A complete tree has no gaps, so it can be stored level by level:

```text
tree:       2   5   4   9   7   8   6
0-based i:  0   1   2   3   4   5   6
```

For a node at index `i`:

```text
left child  = 2*i + 1
right child = 2*i + 2
parent      = (i-1)//2
```

No pointers are needed. Because the tree is complete, its height is
`O(log n)`.

The diagram shows that the visual tree and the array are two views of the
same data. The labels below the cells are array indices.

## Push and pop

To push a value, append it as the last leaf, then swap it upward while it
violates the parent rule. To pop the root, move the last leaf to the root,
remove the last array entry, and swap the new root downward with its better
child.

```text
push: append -> move upward at most one tree height
pop:  replace root -> move downward at most one tree height
top:  read the root without changing anything
```

Therefore `push` and `pop` cost `O(log n)`, while `top` costs `O(1)`. Building
a heap from all values can be done in `O(n)`, although inserting them one by
one gives the simpler `O(n log n)` bound.

why checking and swapping along one path is sufficient.

## Repairing the heap after a pop

After removing the root, move the last leaf into the empty root position.
Compare it with both children and swap with the smaller child. Repeat until
it is no larger than either child.

Choosing the smaller child matters: swapping with the larger child could leave
the new parent larger than its other child. Once again only one root-to-leaf
path is touched, which explains the logarithmic cost.

The next diagram removes 2 from the repaired heap. The last leaf, 9, moves to
the root. It swaps first with 3, the smaller child, and then with 5.

# Heap versus sorted container

A heap is useful when only the current extreme matters. It cannot efficiently
find an arbitrary element, the second-smallest element without removals, or
all values in an interval. If the algorithm needs ordered iteration,
predecessors, or deletion of arbitrary known values, a balanced ordered
container or frequency structure may be more appropriate.

The general recognition question is:

> Do I repeatedly need the smallest or largest item among a collection that
> changes over time?

If yes, a heap may be appropriate. Then state what one heap entry represents
and which operations can insert or remove entries.

Some problems maintain a **frontier** of candidates. In that narrower pattern,
such as merging sorted streams, ask an additional question: after removing one
candidate, can I generate only the candidate that replaces it? This avoids
putting every possible future object into the heap at once.

# Two heaps for medians

Keep the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap:

```text
max(low) <= min(high)
len(low) == len(high) or len(low) == len(high)+1
```

Then the lower median is `max(low)`.

Example insertion sequence:

```text
insert 5: low=[5], high=[]       median=5
insert 1: low=[1], high=[5]      median=1
insert 9: low=[5,1], high=[9]    median=5
insert 2: low=[2,1], high=[5,9]  median=2
```

After every insertion:

1. Put the value in the correct side.
2. Swap tops if order is violated.
3. Rebalance sizes.

A simpler implementation combines the first two steps: compare the new value
with the largest value in `low`. Insert it into `low` if it belongs to the
smaller half, otherwise into `high`. Then rebalance:

```text
if low has two more elements than high:
    move max(low) to high
if high has more elements than low:
    move min(high) to low
```

Why does moving only the top work? If `low` is too large, its maximum is the
only element that should cross into the upper half. Every other value in
`low` is no larger. The symmetric argument holds for `high`.

Each insertion needs only a constant number of heap operations. Therefore the
total cost over `n` inserted values is `O(n log n)`, with `O(n)` stored values.

# Sweep with ending times

To count rooms for intervals, process intervals by start time. A
min-heap stores end times of currently occupied rooms. Before a new
interval starts, pop all rooms whose end time is at most the start.
The heap size is the number of simultaneous intervals.

For half-open intervals `[l,r)`, an interval ending at time `t` does not
overlap an interval starting at `t`. Therefore pop while:

```text
end_time <= next_start
```

For closed intervals `[l,r]`, the condition would be different.

## Why the maximum heap size is the answer

Immediately before inserting `[start, end)`, remove every ending time at most
`start`. What remains is exactly the set of earlier courses overlapping the
new course. After pushing `end`, the heap size is the number of courses active
at that moment.

Any schedule needs at least that many rooms because simultaneous courses
cannot share. Conversely, expired rooms are always reusable, so the sweep
never needs more rooms than this maximum. The lower and upper bounds match.

# K-way merging

If arrays `A` and `B` are sorted, each fixed `i` gives a sorted
stream:

```text
A[i]+B[0], A[i]+B[1], A[i]+B[2], ...
```

Put the first item of every stream in a heap. Repeatedly pop the
smallest sum and push the next sum from the same stream. This is the
same idea as merging many sorted lists.

Worked example:

```text
A = [1, 4]
B = [2, 3, 10]
```

Streams:

```text
i=0: 3, 4, 11
i=1: 6, 7, 14
```

Each heap entry stores three pieces of information:

```text
(pair sum, index in A, index in B)
```

Therefore `(3,0,0)` represents `A[0] + B[0] = 1 + 2 = 3`, while `(6,1,0)`
represents `A[1] + B[0] = 4 + 2 = 6`.

Initially, put only the first sum of each row in the heap:

```text
heap: (3,0,0), (6,1,0)
```

The smallest entry is `(3,0,0)`, so output `3`. This removes the current
representative of row 0. The next unseen sum in that same row uses the next
element of `B`:

```text
A[0] + B[1] = 1 + 3 = 4
```

Push `(4,0,1)`. The heap now contains:

```text
(4,0,1), (6,1,0)
```

The next output is consequently `4`. After removing it, replace it with the
next item of row 0, `(11,0,2)`. The trace begins:

| Output | Removed entry | Replacement | Heap afterward |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 3 | `(3,0,0)` | `(4,0,1)` | 4, 6 |
| 4 | `(4,0,1)` | `(11,0,2)` | 6, 11 |
| 6 | `(6,1,0)` | `(7,1,1)` | 7, 11 |

At every moment, the heap stores the first unseen sum from each row, rather
than storing all `n*m` pair sums.

## Why the popped sum is globally next

For each row, the heap contains its first not-yet-reported sum. Every later
sum in that row is at least this representative because `B` is sorted. The
smallest heap representative is therefore no larger than any unseen sum in
any row. It is safe to output.

After popping row `i`, only that row loses its representative, so push its
next column. This restores the invariant.

The heap has at most `n` entries. Initialization costs `O(n log n)` with
individual pushes, and producing `k` answers costs `O(k log n)`. The total is
`O((n + k) log n)` time and `O(n)` extra memory; it avoids the impossible
`O(nm)` list of all pair sums.

# Optimal merging: repeatedly combine the two smallest

Suppose merging files of sizes `x` and `y` costs `x + y`, and the merged file
may be merged again. An early merge contributes its size to later costs, so
large files should not be created too early.

The greedy rule is:

```text
remove the two smallest current sizes
pay their sum
insert their sum back into the heap
```

For `[2, 3, 4, 6]`:

```text
merge 2 + 3 = 5    total = 5      heap: 4, 5, 6
merge 4 + 5 = 9    total = 14     heap: 6, 9
merge 6 + 9 = 15   total = 29     heap: 15
```

Why are the two smallest safe to merge first? In the final merge tree, every
original size is charged once for each level above its leaf. Two deepest
sibling leaves can be chosen to hold the two smallest weights: exchanging a
larger deep weight with a smaller shallow weight cannot increase the total.
Contracting those two siblings into one combined weight leaves the same
problem on one fewer item. This is the Huffman-coding exchange argument.

There are `n - 1` merges, each using a constant number of heap operations.
The total time is `O(n log n)` and the heap uses `O(n)` memory. Use 64-bit
integers: intermediate sizes and the accumulated cost may exceed 32 bits.

# Python and C++ heap details

Python's `heapq` is a min-heap. For a max-heap, store negative values:

```python
import heapq
low = []
heapq.heappush(low, -x)
largest = -low[0]
```

C++ `priority_queue<int>` is a max-heap by default. For a min-heap:

```cpp
priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq;
```

For pair sums, store all fields needed to generate the next candidate:

```text
(current_sum, i, j)
```

If you store only `current_sum`, you cannot know which next pair to push.

```text
For interval problems, decide whether touching endpoints overlap.
```

# Additional worked decision traces

## Running median: preserve two halves

After every insertion, `low` is a max-heap holding the smaller half and `high`
is a min-heap holding the larger half. Maintain both facts:

```text
every value in low <= every value in high
size(low) == size(high) or size(low) == size(high)+1
```

For prefix `5, 1, 9, 2`, the lower medians are traced below.

```text
insert   low (max heap)   high (min heap)   printed
5        {5}              {}                5
1        {1,5} -> {1}     {5}               1
9        {1}              {5,9} -> move 5   5
2        {1,2}            {5,9}             2
```

The arrows are the rebalance step. Once the two facts hold, exactly
`ceil(prefix_length/2)` values are at most `low.top()`, so it is the requested
lower median. Each push/pop costs `O(log n)`.

## Course rooms: a heap is the active frontier

Sort half-open intervals by start. The min-heap contains end times of courses
that have started but not yet ended. For `(0,10),(5,7),(6,20),(10,12)`:

```text
start interval   remove ends <= start   active end heap after push
0     [0,10)     none                  {10}
5     [5,7)      none                  {7,10}
6     [6,20)     none                  {7,10,20}
10    [10,12)    remove 7,10           {12,20}
```

The maximum heap size is three. The `<=` is essential: half-open intervals
ending at time 10 and starting at time 10 do not overlap.

## K smallest pair sums: merge sorted rows

If both arrays are sorted, each fixed `i` creates a sorted row
`a[i]+b[0], a[i]+b[1], ...`. Seed the heap with each row's first value and
advance only the row that was popped. For `a=[1,4,8]`, `b=[2,3,10]`:

```text
initial heap: (3,row0,col0), (6,row1,col0), (10,row2,col0)
pop 3, push 4; pop 4, push 11; pop 6, push 7; pop 7, push 14
```

Thus the first four sums are `3,4,6,7`. The heap always holds the smallest
unreported element of every nonempty row, so its minimum is globally next.
Only seed `min(n,k)` rows in a generalized variant; the local contract has
`k <= n*m`.

# Implementation and proof habits

**C++.** `priority_queue<T>` is a max-heap; write
`priority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<T>>` for a min-heap. Store pair sums in
`long long`, and store `(sum,row,col)` as a tuple so lexicographic comparison
breaks ties safely.

**Python.** `heapq` is a min-heap. Negate values for a max-heap, and use tuples
such as `(sum,row,col)` rather than custom comparators. Never call `heappop` on
an empty heap; prove the seed/advance invariant first.

# Failure modes, exercises, and workflow

| Problem | Wrong shortcut | Test |
|---|---|---|
| A | sort every prefix | descending input of length `2e5` |
| B | remove ends `< start` | `[0,10)` and `[10,12)` |
| C | seed every pair | two arrays of length `2e5` with small `k` |

1. Prove that moving `high.top()` to `low` repairs both running-median facts.
2. Explain why the room heap size after cleanup equals the number of overlapping
   intervals at the current start time.
3. On paper, list the first five sums for `[0,7]` and `[1,2,9]` using rows.

Answers: the moved element is the smallest large-half value; every remaining
end is strictly after the current start; the sums are `1,2,8,9,9`.

Run `CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/39_heaps_priority_queues/check.py`.
For A compare with a sorted prefix, for B brute-force overlap counts on small
interval sets, and for C enumerate and sort every pair sum when `n,m <= 8`.

Use A to maintain the two-heap size invariant. In B, free rooms before
allocating a new one. In C, make each heap item represent the next unseen pair.
Test duplicate values and equal endpoints.
